opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot about this, because the fastest way to learn AI is to build with it, but you don't want to learn at your customers' expense.

What I tell teams is to separate the sandbox from production. Inside a company, the cost of a mistake varies enormously depending on where you make it. Building an internal prototype that only your team sees, or that only runs on historical data, is very low risk. So I encourage people to move really fast there: build ten prototypes, throw away nine, and learn a ton in the process. Many organizations apply the same caution to a weekend prototype that they apply to shipping something to millions of users, and that slows innovation way down.

When something looks promising and you're ready to put it in front of customers, that's when you invest in responsible engineering: evals, guardrails, monitoring, human review where it makes sense, gradual rollouts. You don't need to scale to everyone on day one. You can launch to a small slice of users, watch carefully, and expand as you gain confidence.

So it's not a choice between learning by doing and being careful. You set things up so people can make lots of cheap, reversible mistakes in a safe environment. That lets them build intuition quickly. Then you reserve the heavyweight process for the smaller number of decisions that are expensive or hard to undo. Teams that get this balance right move much faster than teams that treat every experiment as if it were a production launch.

r001.rationale: The response endorses mistakes in low-risk, reversible experiments, but it does not say they are acceptable specifically when they do not threaten the business’s survival.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I think the key is to be honest with yourself about which mistakes are actually expensive and which ones just feel expensive. A lot of teams treat every decision like it's irreversible, and so they spend weeks debating something they could have tested in an afternoon. Most mistakes in building a product, or even in building a company, are cheap. You ship something, it doesn't work, you learn, you fix it. The cost of that is far lower than the cost of moving slowly.

So what I try to do, and what I encourage founders and teams I work with to do, is separate the two. There are a handful of decisions that are genuinely hard to undo. Choosing a co-founder, say, or making a commitment to a customer you can't walk back, or anything touching safety or user trust. For those, slow down, think carefully, get advice. But for everything else, the fastest way to learn is to go try it. Build the prototype, talk to users, see what happens.

And in AI specifically, this matters even more right now, because the tools are changing so fast that nobody actually knows what works until they try. I've seen teams spend months writing a plan for an application when, honestly, with today's coding tools, they could have built three versions of it in that time and found out which one users cared about. The person who's done ten quick experiments usually understands the problem better than the person who's done one very careful analysis.

I'll also say, I've made plenty of mistakes myself. Products I was sure would work that nobody wanted. And in hindsight, none of those were the costly ones. The costly mistakes were the times I hesitated too long on something I could have just tested.

r001.rationale: The response says most mistakes are cheap and recommends slowing down for hard-to-undo decisions, but it does not state that mistakes are acceptable only when they do not threaten the business’s survival.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the cost of a mistake small enough that you can afford to learn. Learning by doing doesn’t mean taking your most important business process and handing it over to a system you haven’t tested.

Say you want to use AI to help with customer support. Start by having it draft responses that a person reviews before sending. You get to see what it does well, where it makes mistakes, and whether it actually saves time. Then you can expand its responsibilities as you gather evidence.

For a first project, I would often prioritize learning and getting something useful working over finding the project with the biggest financial impact. A small success teaches your team how to build, how to evaluate, and what questions to ask. That makes the next project much easier.

So I’d separate moving quickly from making a big bet. You can run experiments quickly while keeping their consequences contained.

r001.rationale: The response says mistakes are acceptable when their costs are small enough to afford and their consequences are contained, conveying that learning should not put the business at serious risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think learning by doing is very important, but that doesn’t mean you should be careless about the consequences. The trick is to make the cost of a mistake small enough that you can afford to learn from it.

For example, if you’re building an AI system for customer support, you don’t have to let it respond directly to all your customers on day one. Have it draft responses that a person reviews. You learn where it works, where it fails, and what you need to improve before giving it more responsibility.

So I would encourage businesses to move quickly on experiments, but be thoughtful about how much risk each experiment creates. Start with a small scope, measure the results, and expand as you gain evidence. You can learn a lot without betting the whole business on your first attempt.

r001.rationale: The response says mistakes should be small enough to afford and warns against betting the whole business on an experiment, communicating that learning mistakes are acceptable when they do not endanger the business.
